content: The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has expanded its recommendations regarding specific industrial hazards. Previously, these recommendations were relatively silent on behaviors that were narrowly understood as strictly personal health-related issues, such as smoking. However, NIOSH has now adopted a more comprehensive preventive approach. This shift has been driven by an improved understanding of how tobacco use negatively affects occupational diseases and injuries. Equally significant is the evolving societal perspective on the health and economic consequences of tobacco use. For instance, in the past decade, NIOSH criteria documents addressing two lung hazards—refractory ceramic fibers and hexavalent chromium—have included entire sections dedicated to smoking cessation. This inclusion marks a departure from earlier criteria documents, which did not address smoking cessation (refer to Appendix A-2). In a 2004 medical journal article, the Director of NIOSH stated, Smoking is an occupational hazard, both for the worker who smokes and for the nonsmoker who is exposed to it in their workplace.
